implementation_notes: Swift's standard library has no logger, but Apple's swift-log defines the standard chokepoint (the LogHandler protocol) and CryptoKit supplies HMAC<SHA256>, so the idiom is a LogHandler that canonicalises message plus metadata, chains the previous tag and appends to a file the app only appends to; os.Logger/OSLog remains the operational sink it is good at. Use this realisation when the evidence must be verifiable outside Apple's unified log, whose storage you cannot key yourself; the hand-written writer is justified when even swift-log must not be a dependency (a small in-process appender).
pitfalls: LogHandler methods are called from arbitrary queues and swift-log bootstraps are process-wide: guard the chain state (NSLock or an actor) and configure exactly one handler per log destination.
os.Logger writes to the unified log, which offers no per-application key and no custom authenticator - using it as the tamper-evident store silently drops the property you designed for.
HMAC<SHA256> rejects unusable keys and CryptoKit failures are thrown, not ignored: validate key material at startup so the first audit record is not the first failure point.
